name: anti-slop
summary: An opinionated set of Oxlint rules, copied into your repository rather than installed, that rejects “low-evidence” TypeScript and JavaScript such as `unknown` parameters, chained type assertions and ad hoc `typeof` checks.
intro: Despite the name, anti-slop checks code, not prose. It is one engineer’s personal rule set, a JavaScript plugin for Oxlint (the linter in the Oxc project), and its README says plainly that it reflects the author’s preferences rather than a universal standard. Most of its 18 generic rules target code that claims more than it can prove: `no-chained-type-assertions` rejects `input as object as User`, `no-unknown-parameters` and `no-unknown-returns` reject `unknown` in function contracts, `no-runtime-typeof` asks for parsing at the boundary instead of scattered `typeof` checks, and `require-safety-comment-for-type-assertion` demands a `// SAFETY:` comment explaining each `as`. Others reject Jest and Vitest module mocking, `Reflect.get`, eager `filter().map()` chains and copying the accumulator inside `reduce`. A separate opt-in group of five rules covers code written with the Effect library.

There is deliberately no npm package. You copy the `src/` folder into your repository, register it under `jsPlugins` in `oxlint.config.ts`, and then own and edit the rules; an agent skill (`npx skills add dmmulroy/anti-slop`) lets a coding agent do the copy, configuration and later three-way-merge updates. The rules use Oxlint’s syntax-tree and scope APIs, not the TypeScript type checker, so they resolve type aliases within one file but can’t see imported types or call signatures from other files.
strengths: Pushes TypeScript code toward parsed, explicitly typed boundaries, which catches the casts and `unknown` plumbing that slip through ordinary lint rules
Runs at Oxlint speed, with each rule documented by examples of what it rejects and what to write instead
Vendored on purpose, so a team can read every rule and change the policy to fit
limits: One person’s taste, not a standard: several rules, such as banning `typeof` checks or module mocking, will clash with many codebases
No npm package: you copy the code (tagged up to v0.1.2) and maintain your copy, and `oxlint` and `@oxlint/plugins` must be pinned to the same exact version
Single-file analysis without a type checker, so some patterns across modules go unseen

snippet.title: Two rules from the README: rejected code, then what passes
source: // no-array-filter-map: two eager passes over the array
const id = value as UserId;            // rejected
// SAFETY: parseUserId validated the identifier before branding it.
const userId = value as UserId;        // allowed

story: Dillon Mulroy, a software engineer at Cloudflare, extracted the rules he uses with his own work, projects and team into a standalone Oxlint plugin in August 2026 and added an opt-in Effect rule group a week later. The repository has since gathered over 5,000 GitHub stars, and outside contributors have added Effect rules, tests and refinements to the spacing rule.

choices.choice: Vendor the rules instead of publishing a package
choices.why: The rules encode one team’s policy; copying them makes each adopter read and own the policy, and community packages can manage their own releases.

choices.choice: Build on Oxlint’s JavaScript plugin API
choices.why: Rules written in TypeScript against Oxlint’s ESTree and scope APIs run inside the fast Rust linter without a TypeScript type-checking pass.

timeline.text: August: rules extracted into a standalone Oxlint plugin
August: opt-in Effect rules; contributors add more by September
